en: Points of Controversy:
The Great Fifty-Section,
Ninth Chapter
Is it not the case that speech does not accord with the mind?
Yes, it is so.
Is speech that of one without contact, speech that of one without feeling, speech that of one without perception, speech that of one without volition, or speech that of one without mind?
Certainly not; it should not be stated thus...

Is it not the case, rather, that speech is that of one with contact, speech that of one with feeling, speech that of one with perception, speech that of one with volition, and speech that of one with mind?
“Yes.
“If speech belongs to one who possesses contact … [and so on] … if speech belongs to one who possesses mind, then indeed, sir, you should not say:”
“Speech is not according to the mind.
Is it the case that speech is not according to the mind?
Yes, it is.
Is it the speech of one who does not turn back [the mind], ...pe...
the speech of one who is without effort, ...pe... the speech of one who does not intend?
One should certainly not say so, ...pe...
Is it not the case that there is speech when turning back, speech when applying attention, and speech when making an aspiration?
Yes, it is so.
If there is speech when turning back, speech when applying attention, and speech when making an aspiration, then indeed, you should not say: [that there is no such thing].
“Speech is not in accordance with the mind.
Is it the case that speech is not in accordance with the mind?
Yes, it is.
Is it not the case that speech is originated by mind, co-nascent with mind, and arises simultaneously with mind?
Yes, it is.
If speech is indeed originated by mind, co-nascent with mind, and arises simultaneously with mind, then surely you must not say:
“Speech is not according to the mind.
Is it the case that speech is not according to the mind?
Yes, it is.

"Does one speak without desiring to speak, does one converse without desiring to converse, does one address others without desiring to address them, and does one engage in discourse without desiring to engage in discourse?
"One should not say so...

"...Is it not the case that one speaks because one desires to speak, converses because one desires to converse, addresses others because one desires to address them, and engages in discourse because one desires to engage in discourse?"
“Yes.

[The opponent asks: “If one speaks because one wishes to speak, explains because one wishes to explain, addresses because one wishes to address, and converses because one wishes to converse, then surely it should not be said that ‘speech does not follow the mind.’”
Is it not to be said that speech does not accord with the mind?
Yes, it is so.

Is it not the case that there is someone who, intending to say one thing, says another; who, intending to speak of one thing, speaks of another; who, intending to address one thing, addresses another; who, intending to communicate one thing, communicates another? Yes, there is.
Indeed, there is someone who, intending to say one thing, says another... [and so on].
“If one speaks something else [thinking], ‘I shall speak something else,’ then indeed it must be said of him:
‘Speech does not accord with the mind.
The discussion on speech not being in accordance with the mind is finished.
